title: Harmony @Huailan: battery settings changed to buy less from the grid
lede: Our review of this Chiang Mai eco-lodge's 10 kW solar + battery system showed its battery settings were costing money. On 2 November 2026 we changed them remotely. Here is what changed, in plain words.
bullets: Before: the battery was held at 40% most of the day and night, and pushed up to 80% from 09:00 to 17:00.
Before: grid charging was on in every time slot, so the inverter bought grid power in the morning to fill the battery just before the sun could do it for free.
Now: the battery can run down to 25% in every time slot before the house draws from the grid.
Now: grid charging is off in every slot, so the battery is charged by the sun only. Time of Use stays on and selling to the grid stays off.
The inverter confirmed the new settings at 09:00 on 2 November 2026.
Expected result: less grid electricity bought, especially early in the morning, and more of the battery used every night.
Trade-off: in a night-time blackout there may be as little as 25% left in the battery; the owner can raise the night slots to 40% if backup matters more than savings.
thailand_note: Many hybrid systems in Thailand are left on installer default settings. Checking the battery and grid-charge settings against how the building actually uses power is a free way to cut the electricity bill.

title: Harmony @Huailan Ecolodge: how the lodge uses its solar power
lede: We reviewed a month of 5-minute readings from this Chiang Mai eco-lodge's 10 kWp solar and battery system. The system works well, but two free setting changes and one large appliance explain most of the grid power it buys.
bullets: No faults or alarms: the solar system works well.
Use is up: about 14 kWh a day in October 2026 (+12% on last year), and grid purchases up 52%.
Always-on loads (fridges, freezers, pumps, Wi-Fi, outdoor lights) never drop below about 0.45–0.55 kW and make up roughly 80% of daily use.
About once a day a very large two-phase load of 11–12 kW switches on for a few minutes, early morning or late evening, most likely water heating.
After about noon the battery is full and roughly 6–8 kWh of free solar a day goes unused.
Most grid buying came from two settings: the battery stopped at 40% instead of 25%, and it refilled from the grid every morning. Both were changed on 2 November 2026.
Recommendations: move big loads to 11:00–16:00, find and manage the large heater, check always-on loads, and decide on more battery only after watching the busy season.
thailand_note: Many Thai hybrid systems are left on default battery settings. A monitoring review like this one often finds savings without buying any new equipment.

title: Harmony @Huailan Ecolodge: keeping the lodge, water pump and hot water running in a power cut
lede: The lodge asked whether its existing 10 kW solar and battery system could keep everything running during a blackout, including the hot water heater and water pump. Here is our advice in plain words.
bullets: The lodge and the water pump can be backed up with the system it already has, after rewiring circuits to the backup side.
The current hot water heater cannot: at about 11–12 kW it is above the inverter's 10 kW total and 5 kW per-phase limits and would shut the system down.
In a power cut the inverter has three limits: 10 kW in total, 5 kW on any one phase, and the energy stored in the battery.
Option A (recommended): replace the heater with a heat-pump water heater and hot-water tank, so lodge, pump and hot water all run in a blackout and the monthly bill also falls.
Option B: smaller heating elements with a storage tank, so heating stays within the inverter's limits.
Option C: keep the current heater and add a second 10 kW inverter plus more battery; no change in habits, but by far the most expensive.
For very long cuts of a day or more, a small generator can be connected as an extra safety net.
thailand_note: Water heaters are often the biggest single load in Thai resorts and homestays. Sizing hot water to the inverter is usually cheaper than sizing the inverter to the heater.
